dialogue.literal_gloss: Amai [mother] • vakati [they (past) ti] • Chiuya [come now!] • kuno [here / to this place] • undibatsire [undibatsire]

grammar_notes.title: Giving Commands & Polite Requests ('Chiuya')
grammar_notes.content: Notice the command verb 'Chiuya' in this sentence. In Shona, a direct command to one person (singular) is simply the verb stem ending in '-a'—for example, 'Vhara!' ('Close!'), 'Tora!' ('Take!'), or 'Huya!' ('Come!'). When speaking to more than one person, or when showing polite respect to an adult, you add '-i' to the end, changing '-a' to '-ai' (as in 'Huyai!' = 'Come!' or 'Batai!' = 'Catch/Hold!'). Adding the prefix 'chi-' (as in 'Chiuya' or 'Chigara') means 'Do it right now'.
grammar_notes.rule: Singular Command: Verb stem (-a) [Huya! / Tora!] | Polite or Plural Command: Verb stem + -i (-ai) [Huyai! / Torai!]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('vakati')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vakati' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: How Shona Sentences Fit Together (Subject + Tense + Verb)
grammar_notes.content: In 'Amai vakati, "Chiuya kuno undibatsire."', notice how a single Shona verb word packs together who is doing the action (the subject prefix), when it happens (the tense marker), and the action itself (the verb stem). Once you recognize the building blocks at the start of the verb—like 'ndi-' (I), 'u-' (you), 'ti-' (we), or 'va-' (they)—you can immediately spot the subject even when no separate pronoun word is used!
grammar_notes.rule: [Who (Subject Prefix)] + [When (Tense Marker)] + [Action (Verb Root)] -> e.g., ti- (we) + -cha- (will) + -svika (arrive) = tichasvika

cultural_notes.title: Household Cooperation, Politeness & Consideration at Home
cultural_notes.content: Daily home life in Shona culture revolves around mutual assistance ('kubatsirana') and consideration for others in the household. When asking a family member to help lift something heavy ('undibatsire kusimudza'), open or close a door ('musuwo') or window ('hwindo'), or speak softly ('kuzevezera') while a child is sleeping ('mwana akarara'), polite phrasing keeps household life warm and harmonious.

active_exercises.correct_answer: Take the water and drink it.

Choose the natural English meaning of this new sentence: 'Vana vanoda kudya chingwa nemukaka mangwanani.'
options: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
We bought sugar, salt, and vegetables yesterday.
Father is cooking meat and sadza for dinner tonight.
The bread has run out so I am going to the shop.
active_exercises.correct_answer: The children want to eat bread and milk in the morning.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Vana' = 'The children', 'vanoda kudya' = 'want to eat', 'chingwa nemukaka' = 'bread and milk', 'mangwanani' = 'in the morning'.
